title: How many digits must the milk packet code have?
description: A dairy wants a different code on each of its milk packets, using only the digits zero to nine. The video counts the codes that any number of digit slots can make and finds how many slots are enough, the same way as the digit lock.
teaching_notes: One idea: a code of some number of digit slots gives ten multiplied by itself that many times, so we compare powers of ten with the number of packets. Watch for students who divide the number of packets by ten, or who stop at the first power of ten that looks close.

video_script.why: A learner uses the digit slots of the digit lock to find how many slots are enough for a given number of codes.
video_script.substitution: the book's own dairy plan of eight and a half billion packets
video_script.anchor: the dairy's milk packets, each with its own code
video_script.payoff_line: Ten to the power ten is enough for every packet
maths_rules: check: 9 digits give 1000000000 codes, which is too few
video_script.design: One idea: n digit slots give ten to the power n codes. The powers of ten are tried one after another against the number of packets, and the digit count only appears at the answer.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; rows of milk packets, each with an empty code box; the plan: 8.5 billion packets in a year

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='dairy'/>A dairy plans to make eight and a half billion packets of milk in a year.
<bookmark mark='code'/>Every packet needs its own code, made only from the digits zero to nine.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many digits should the code have?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: the digit lock with slots, each slot with the digits 0 to 9, beside the code box of a packet

marks.lock: the digit lock from the earlier example is set beside the code box
marks.slot: each slot of the code box shows ten digits

narration: <bookmark mark='lock'/>We solve this the same way as the digit lock in your book.
<bookmark mark='slot'/>A code is like the lock. Every slot has ten choices.

beats.on_screen: Given: 8.5 billion packets; each slot of a code is a digit from 0 to 9

marks.given: the number of packets and the digits 0 to 9 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, eight and a half billion packets. Every slot of a code is a digit from zero to nine.

beats.on_screen: To find: the fewest slots that give a different code for every packet

marks.find: the words fewest slots with a different code for every packet are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the fewest slots that give every packet a different code.

beats.on_screen: n slots: 10 x 10 x ... x 10 with n tens = 10^n codes

marks.tens: one 10 is written under each of n slots

narration: <bookmark mark='tens'/>Step one, count the codes for some number of slots. Call that number n.
<bookmark mark='power'/>Each slot has ten choices, so n slots give ten to the power n codes.
<bookmark mark='number'/>Step two, write the packets with powers of ten. Eight and a half billion is eight point five times one billion.
<bookmark mark='power'/>One billion is ten to the power nine. The packets are eight point five times that.

marks.few: a cross marks 1000000000 as too few

narration: <bookmark mark='nine'/>Step three, try ten to the power nine. That is one billion codes.
<bookmark mark='few'/>One billion is less than eight and a half billion, so that is too few.

marks.next: one more slot is added: 10^10 = 10000000000 appears
marks.enough: a tick marks 10000000000 as more than 8500000000

narration: <bookmark mark='next'/>Step four, check one more slot. Ten to the power ten is ten billion codes.
<bookmark mark='enough'/>Ten billion is more than eight and a half billion, so every packet gets its own code.
<bookmark mark='pay'/>Ten to the power ten is enough for every packet.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The code should have ten digits.
